evidence.title: Baghdad (Madinat al-Salam): Abbasid caliphal embassy departure (21 June 921 CE)
evidence.summary: Caliph al-Muqtadir dispatched an embassy headed by the eunuch Susan al-Rassi—with jurist/chronicler Ahmad ibn Fadlan reading letters and overseeing gifts—in response to Volga Bulgar ruler Almish ibn Shilki's request for Islamic instruction and fortress funds against the Khazars.
evidence.limits: Ibn Fadlan states exact Islamic calendar dates; later YAqut and the 1923 Mashhad manuscript preserve only the outward and middle sections of the report, breaking off during the Khazar excursus.
evidence.dateBasis: Exact date preserved in the Mashhad Manuscript of Ibn Fadlan's Risala (11 Safar 309 AH).

evidence.title: Hamadan & Rayy (Jibal corridor): Abbasid trunk road into northern Iran
evidence.summary: The delegation pushed rapidly east along the Khorasan Highway through Nahrawan, Hulwan, Kermanshah, and Hamadan to Rayy (near modern Tehran), pausing 11 days for Ahmad ibn 'Ali before crossing into Samanid territory.
evidence.limits: Rayy was an established administrative relay city; exact intermediate campsite coordinates between Zagros passes are approximate.
evidence.dateBasis: Travel stages timed relative to the Baghdad departure and Rayy 11-day halt in the Risala.

evidence.title: Nishapur & Merv (Khorasan): Samanid frontier escort
evidence.summary: Entering Khorasan—then troubled by political tension over Rayy and the Shi'i Alids in Tabaristan—the embassy hid its insignia through Daylamite-contested roads until meeting Samanid commander Hammuyah ibn 'Ali at Nishapur and crossing the Karakum from Merv to Amul on the Oxus.
evidence.limits: Route anchor uses the major caravan cities Nishapur and Merv named in the Risala.
evidence.dateBasis: Stage sequence dated in the Risala between Rayy and Bukhara.

evidence.title: Bukhara (Transoxania): Samanid court & unpaid Paykand dinars
evidence.summary: At Bukhara the embassy met vizier Abu 'Abdallah al-Jayhani and the young Emir Nasr II ibn Ahmad. Ibn Fadlan waited 28 days for 4,000 dinars promised from estates at Paykand; when the agent returned empty-handed under mounting diplomatic pressure, the mission departed without the fortress money.
evidence.limits: The missing 4,000 dinars later sparked bitter confrontation at the Bulgar court in May 922 CE.
evidence.dateBasis: Court audience and 28-day delay recorded in Ibn Fadlan's Risala.

evidence.title: Kath (Afrighid Khwarazm): river crossing & Khwarazmshah audience
evidence.summary: Embarking down the Oxus (Amu Darya) from Paykand/Amul in hired vessels, the mission reached Kath on the river's right bank. Afrighid ruler Muhammad ibn 'Iraq examined al-Muqtadir's diploma and initially tried to dissuade the envoys from braving Oghuz tribesmen and steppe cold before granting safe-conduct.
evidence.limits: Archaeological shifting of the lower Oxus channels leaves early-10th-century Kath's suburban landing zones approximate.
evidence.dateBasis: Risala chronology immediately prior to winter stay in Gurganj.

evidence.title: Gurganj / Old Urgench (Khwarazm): three-month freeze & jurists' retreat
evidence.dateLabel: Nov 921 – 3 Mar 922 CE (4 Shawwal 309 AH departure)
evidence.summary: When the Oxus froze to a thickness of 17 spans, the envoys wintered in Gurganj (Konye-Urgench). Here the jurists and religious teacher panicked over reports of severed roads and brutal cold and turned back, leaving Ibn Fadlan, Susan al-Rassi, Tekin al-Turki, and Baris al-Saqlabi to carry camel-hide folding boats onto the spring thaw caravan.
evidence.limits: Ibn Fadlan himself emphasized the frostbite and cracked bronze vessels during this overwintering.
evidence.dateBasis: Exact spring departure date (3–4 March 922 CE) in the Mashhad Risala.

evidence.title: Ust-Urt Plateau & Emba Steppe: Oghuz (al-Ghuzziyya) tribal council
evidence.summary: Climbing the steep stony scarp onto the Ust-Urt Plateau in snowstorms, the caravan encountered Oghuz Turks (*al-Ghuzziyya*). Ibn Fadlan recorded felt tents, marriage bridewealth in Khwarazmian garments and sheep, wooden funerary effigies (*balbals*), and an emergency steppe assembly under commander Etrek that debated executing or ransoming the Abbasid envoys.
evidence.limits: Steppe coordinates mark the Ust-Urt/Emba caravan zone; nomadic camps shifted seasonally.
evidence.dateBasis: Stage log between Zamjan gate and Emba/Yaik rivers in Spring 922 CE.

evidence.title: Yaik (Ural) & Southern Ural crossings: Pechenegs & Bashkirs
evidence.summary: Fording the swollen Ural (Yaik) River using inflated leather skins and camel-hide craft alongside horses, the mission crossed Pecheneg grazing grounds near a salt lake and guarded Bashkir forests—describing phallic and animal tutelary wooden emblems—before crossing the Samara, Sok, and Cheremshan tributaries toward the Kama confluence.
evidence.limits: Specific river names vary slightly across manuscript editors; coordinates anchor the middle Ural–Samara steppe corridor.
evidence.dateBasis: Continuous daily river-crossing journal of Dhu al-Hijjah 309 AH (April 922 CE).

evidence.title: Bolgar & Three Lakes Royal Camp (Middle Volga): arrival 12 May 922 CE
evidence.summary: After nearly eleven months from Baghdad, the envoys reached King (Yiltawar) Almish ibn Shilki (adopting the name Ja'far ibn 'Abdallah), who knelt during Ibn Fadlan's public reading of al-Muqtadir's letter while courtiers showered silver dirhams. Ibn Fadlan recorded the short subarctic white nights, red-cloud auroral battles, giant bone finds (likely Pleistocene megafauna), silver-dirham-funded sable fur trade, and tense arguments over the missing 4,000 fortress dinars.
evidence.limits: Three Lakes camp sat along small oxbow lakes south of later stone masonry Bolgar; modern excavations show Bolgar grew from seasonal tent markets into a major fortified trading town.
evidence.dateBasis: Exact Risala arrival date (12 Muharram 310 AH) corroborated by Samanid dirham hoards along the Middle Volga.

evidence.title: Rus' (al-Rusiyya) Trading Camp on the Volga: chieftain ship cremation & realism vs. legend
evidence.summary: At the river market Ibn Fadlan observed Swedish/Varangian Rus' merchants mooring wooden longships to sell marten furs and Slavic slaves (*Saqaliba*). He documented their blue-green wood-ash body tattoos, broad Frankish swords, silver dirham neck-torques (one per 10,000 dirhams earned), morning washbasin habit, wooden mooring posts, and a full 10-day chieftain ship-cremation overseen by a senior ritualist called the 'Angel of Death.' There are no Neanderthal 'Wendol' mist-dwellers in the historical text—that plot element was Michael Crichton's 1976 novelistic fusion with Beowulf.
evidence.limits: Archaeology across Volga-Baltic river cemeteries confirms Viking-Age boat cremations and Samanid silver hoards; exact mooring spot along the Bolgar riverfront is unlocated.
evidence.dateBasis: Firsthand eyewitness account in sections 80–93 of the Mashhad manuscript.

evidence.title: Atil (Itil, Lower Volga Delta): Khazar Khaganate & diplomatic horizon
evidence.summary: Although Ibn Fadlan's surviving Mashhad text breaks off inside an account of the Khazar Khaganate (the Khagan, Khagan-Beg, 25 wives including King Almish's hostage daughter, one sable-skin tax per Bulgar household, and the retaliatory demolition of Atil's Friday mosque minaret in 922 CE), the whole Abbasid embassy was driven by Volga Bulgaria's attempt to break free from Khazar suzerainty.
evidence.limits: Whether Ibn Fadlan traveled back south via Atil or returned via Khwarazm is uncertain because the closing folios of the Mashhad manuscript are lost.
evidence.dateBasis: 922 CE religious retaliation incident preserved in the final surviving Khazar paragraphs of the Risala.

evidence.title: Zhang Qian's departure from Chang'an (Xi'an): opening the Silk Road diplomacy (138–114 BCE)
evidence.summary: Han Emperor Wu sent imperial envoy Zhang Qian west from Chang'an in 138 BCE to forge an alliance with the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu. After 10+ years of Xiongnu captivity and a heroic escape across the Pamirs, his 126 BCE return gave Han courts detailed intelligence on Central Asia, Parthia, and India, sparking official Hexi Corridor and Wusun missions.
evidence.limits: Dates reflect astronomical conversion (138 BCE = -137) based on Sima Qian's Shiji Ch. 123; exact departure month is unknown.
evidence.dateBasis: Han court chronicles (Shiji Chapter 123, Han Shu Chapter 61).

evidence.title: Fergana (Dayuan) & Bactria (Daxia): Zhang Qian's Central Asian intelligence (129–126 BCE)
evidence.summary: Reaching the Fergana Valley, Kangju (Sogdiana), and Yuezhi camps north of the Oxus near Balkh (Daxia), Zhang Qian documented fortified Greco-Bactrian walled markets, 'heavenly horses,' grapevines/alfalfa, and astonished himself by spotting Sichuan Qiong bamboo staffs and Shu cloth that had already traveled via Yunnan and India (*Shendu*).
evidence.limits: Coordinates anchor Balkh/Oxus Bactrian core; Zhang Qian also visited Dayuan in the Fergana Valley.
evidence.dateBasis: Approximate 129–126 BCE western residence prior to his return to Chang'an in 126 BCE.

evidence.title: Charax Spasinu / Tiaozhi (Persian Gulf): Han envoy Gan Ying (97 CE)
evidence.summary: Dispatched by Eastern Han Protector-General Ban Chao, envoy Gan Ying marched west across Arsacid Parthia (*Anxi*) to *Tiaozhi* (Charax Spasinu at the head of the Persian Gulf). Seeking maritime passage around Arabia to Roman Syria (*Daqin*), Parthian sailors warned him of three-month-to-three-year headwinds and longing for home; Gan Ying turned back after compiling the earliest surviving Chinese report on Roman governance, paved post-roads, and Mesopotamia.
evidence.limits: Identification of Tiaozhi with Charax Spasinu / Mesene near the Tigris–Euphrates mouth follows Hill (2009) and standard Han historical geography.
evidence.dateBasis: Dated explicitly to the 9th year of Yongyuan (97 CE) in Hou Hanshu Chapter 88.

evidence.title: Faxian at Pataliputra & Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka): 15-year overland-and-sea Vinaya quest (399–414 CE)
evidence.summary: Setting out from Chang'an at age ~65 across the Taklamakan's 'River of Sand' and the Karakorum suspension bridges, Buddhist monk Faxian spent six years in northern India studying Sanskrit at Pataliputra and Tamralipti, then copied sacred texts for two years at Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka) before enduring a 90-day storm voyage across the Java Sea to landfall at Laoshan (Shandong) in 412/413 CE (*Foguoji*).
evidence.limits: Single anchor at Anuradhapura marks his two-year maritime terminus in Sri Lanka; full itinerary spanned Afghanistan to Java.
evidence.dateBasis: Self-dated departure (399 CE), Sri Lanka stay (410–411 CE), and return to Nanjing (414 CE) in Foguoji.

evidence.title: Xuanzang through Gaochang, Tokmak & Samarkand (629–630 CE)
evidence.summary: Defying an imperial Tang travel ban in 629 CE, monk Xuanzang crossed the Gobi Desert, received royal patronage at Gaochang (Turpan), met Western Turkic Khagan Tong Yabghu near Suyab (Tokmak), and observed Zoroastrian and Sogdian towns around Samarkand before descending through the Iron Gates and Bamiyan into India.
evidence.limits: Samarkand coordinate anchors his Transoxanian transit described in the biography (*Da Ci'en Si Sanzang Fashi Zhuan*) and *Da Tang Xiyu Ji*.
evidence.dateBasis: Dated Tang Zhenguan era itinerary (629–630 CE).

evidence.title: Xuanzang at Nalanda Mahavihara & Kannauj: Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (631–645 CE)
evidence.summary: Studying Yogacara philosophy under Silabhadra at Nalanda and traveling throughout India from Kashmir to Kanchipuram and Bengal, Xuanzang debated at Emperor Harsha's 643 CE Kannauj assembly and returned across the Pamirs to Chang'an in 645 CE with 657 Sanskrit texts and Emperor Taizong-commissioned encyclopedia *Da Tang Xiyu Ji* covering over 110 states.
evidence.limits: Monument measurements and monastic headcounts in the Xiyu Ji combine firsthand surveys with regional reports.
evidence.dateBasis: 637/638 CE Nalanda residence, 643 CE Kannauj convocation, and 645 CE Chang'an return.

evidence.title: Yijing at Srivijaya (Palembang, Sumatra) & Sea Route to Nalanda (671–695 CE)
evidence.summary: Sailing aboard a Persian merchant vessel from Guangzhou in 671 CE, Tang monk Yijing studied Sanskrit grammar in the maritime kingdom of Srivijaya (Palembang), spent ten years at Nalanda (675–685 CE), and returned via Srivijaya again for four years to compile biographical records of 56 fellow South Sea Chinese/Korean/Central Asian pilgrims and detailed medical/monastic ethnographies.
evidence.limits: Srivijaya harbor anchorage around modern Palembang reflects consensus archaeological–textual identification.
evidence.dateBasis: Sailing years (671 CE) and Luoyang return (695 CE) in Yijing's surviving works.

evidence.title: Du Huan in Abbasid Kufa & Iraq (Jingxingji, 751–761 CE)
evidence.summary: Captured by Abbasid and Allied forces alongside Tang troops at the 751 CE Battle of Talas, scholar-soldier Du Huan spent over a decade in western Asia (*Yajuluo* / Kufa and the early Abbasid heartland), documenting Arab/Muslim ritual life, Friday prayer, bazaar crafts, and named Chinese silk weavers (Fan Shu, Liu Ci) and painters (Le Huan, Lü Li) working alongside papermakers in Iraq (*Jingxingji*, preserved via his uncle Du You's *Tongdian*).
evidence.limits: Only fragments quoted in Du You's Tongdian survive; exact intermediate travels through Syria (*Fulin*) and Iran remain partial.
evidence.dateBasis: Captured 751 CE (Battle of Talas); returned by merchant vessel to Guangzhou in 762 CE.

evidence.title: Du Huan's Molin & Laobosa (Eritrea / Red Sea Africa): first Chinese eyewitness in Africa (c. 758–762 CE)
evidence.summary: Before boarding an Arabian Sea trading junk back to Guangzhou in 762 CE, Du Huan visited *Molin* (identified by Smidt and Silk Road scholars with Red Sea coastal Eritrea/Adulis or Aksumite highlands, reached southwest across the desert or sea from Egypt/Mecca), describing high-altitude heat, dry grain/date subsistence, dark-skinned inhabitants riding horses, and three distinct religious communities—making him the earliest Chinese traveler with a verifiable firsthand African account.
evidence.limits: Scholarly debate places Molin between coastal Eritrea/Aksum and southern Nubia/Makuria; coordinate marks the Zula/Adulis Red Sea anchorage.
evidence.dateBasis: Prior to Du Huan's maritime return to Guangzhou in 762 CE (*Tongdian* ch. 193).

evidence.title: Rabban Bar Sauma & Markos: Beijing (Khanbaliq) to Ilkhanid Iran (1275–1280 CE)
evidence.summary: Born in Kublai Khan's capital Zhongdu/Khanbaliq (Beijing) to an Ongud Christian family, monk Rabban Bar Sauma and his disciple Markos crossed Shaanxi, Tangut lands, Khotan, Kashgar, Khorasan, and Maragheh to Baghdad, where Markos was elected Catholicos Patriarch Yahballaha III of the Church of the East in 1281 CE.
evidence.limits: Primary biography survives in a Syriac summary rather than Bar Sauma's lost original Persian diary.
evidence.dateBasis: East-to-West overland transit (c. 1275/1276–1280 CE) ahead of Markos's 1281 patriarchal election.

evidence.title: Rabban Bar Sauma in Constantinople, Rome, Paris & Bordeaux (1287–1288 CE): Beijing envoy in Europe
evidence.summary: Dispatched by Ilkhan Arghun in 1287 CE to explore an Ilkhanid–European alliance, the Beijing-born monk sailed from Trebizond to Constantinople (meeting Emperor Andronikos II and touring Hagia Sophia), witnessed a naval battle off Naples and a June 1287 eruption of Mount Etna, debated theology with Roman cardinals during the papal interregnum, met King Philip IV in Paris (touring Sainte-Chapelle and Paris scholars), celebrated Eucharist before King Edward I of England at Bordeaux in Gascony, and later received Pope Nicholas IV's blessing in Rome before returning to Baghdad.
evidence.limits: European monarchs offered warm receptions without launching the proposed joint Syrian crusade.
evidence.dateBasis: Syriac chronicle and European court records fixing his Naples (June 1287), Paris (Sept 1287), and Rome (Spring 1288) stops.

evidence.title: Wang Dayuan from Quanzhou (Zayton): Yuan private merchant voyages across two seas (1330–1339 CE)
evidence.summary: Sailing decades before Zheng He aboard private Fujian and Quanzhou merchant junks (1330–1334 and 1337–1339 CE), scholar Wang Dayuan authored the *Daoyi Zhilüe* ('Brief Account of the Island Barbarians,' 1349) profiling nearly 100 ports across Southeast Asia, Sri Lanka, Bengal, Malabar, Hormuz, Mecca, and East Africa (*Ts'eng-yao-lo* / Zanzibar region), noting monsoon sailing winds, pepper prices, and ceramic exports—alongside earliest Chinese geographical notice of Timor and possibly northern Australia's Timor Sea periphery.
evidence.limits: Distinguishing ports Wang Dayuan personally visited from secondary ports gathered in Calicut and Hormuz requires textual comparison.
evidence.dateBasis: Internal Yuan Zhishun/Zhiyuan voyage spans documented in the 1349/1350 preface of Daoyi Zhilüe.

evidence.title: Zheng He & Ma Huan: Ming Treasure Fleets to Sri Lanka, Hormuz, Aden & Malindi (1405–1433 CE)
evidence.summary: Commanded by Muslim Hui eunuch admiral Zheng He with translators and chroniclers Ma Huan (*Yingyai Shenglan*), Fei Xin (*Xingcha Shenglan*), and Gong Zhen, seven Ming imperial fleets totaling scores of multi-deck treasure and escort ships sailed from Nanjing and Liujiagang across Champa, Java, Melaka, Galle (raising the 1409–1411 trilingual Chinese–Tamil–Persian stele), Calicut, Hormuz, Mecca (envoy branch), Aden, Mogadishu, Brava, and Malindi—returning diplomatic envoys and an East African giraffe presented to Emperor Yongle in 1414.
evidence.limits: Ships clearly stopped along the Swahili Coast around Malindi/Mombasa; speculative claims of global or Americas circumnavigation are not supported by Ming archives or archaeology.
evidence.dateBasis: Ming Veritable Records, Liujiagang/Changle stelae (1431), and the 1409 Galle Trilingual Inscription.

evidence.title: Xu Xiake's Southwest survey: Guizhou–Guangxi karst & Yangtze Jinsha headwaters (1607–1640 CE)
evidence.summary: Instead of imperial diplomacy, Ming private geographer Xu Hongzu (Xu Xiake, 1587–1641) walked across 16 provinces for over three decades keeping daily empirical logs (*Xu Xiake Youji*). Measuring over 100 limestone caverns and sinkholes across Guangxi, Guizhou, and Yunnan, he laid foundations of karst geomorphology and proved through field hydrography in Lijiang/Jinsha that the Jinsha River—not the shorter Min River asserted in classical *Shujing* tradition—was the true main upper course of the Yangtze.
evidence.limits: Posthumous compilation preserved ~600,000 characters; coordinates anchor Lijiang / Jinsha River survey area in northern Yunnan (1639).
evidence.dateBasis: Dated daily travel diary entries from 1613–1640 CE (Yunnan Jinsha entries 1638–1639).

waves.title: Ibn Fadlan embassy leg 1: Baghdad through Rayy, Nishapur & Merv to Bukhara (921 CE)
waves.summary: Caliph al-Muqtadir's mission traveled post-roads along the Khorasan Highway across the Zagros, Jibal, Nishapur, and the Karakum crossing to the Samanid capital of Bukhara.
waves.limits: Schematic corridor connecting named Risala cities; not a continuous GPS track.

waves.title: Ibn Fadlan embassy leg 2: Bukhara via Kath to winter quarters at Gurganj (921–922 CE)
waves.summary: Riverboat journey down the Amu Darya to Kath and Gurganj, where a three-month severe freeze split the party as religious jurists retreated.
waves.limits: Amu Darya channel courses have shifted historically.

waves.title: Ibn Fadlan embassy leg 3: Ust-Urt, Oghuz–Pecheneg–Bashkir steppe to Bolgar (Spring 922 CE)
waves.summary: 69-day spring caravan trek across frozen deserts, Oghuz encampments, swollen Ural/Kama tributaries using folding camel-hide boats, arriving at Three Lakes and Bolgar on 12 May 922 CE.
waves.limits: Ust-Urt scarp and river-crossing points represent approximate caravan line reconstructed from Risala river names.

waves.title: Volga silver–fur axis: Bolgar, Rus' river landings & Khazar Atil (922–925 CE)
waves.summary: The Volga trade highway documented by Ibn Fadlan: Scandinavian-Rus' longships descending to Bolgar carrying northern furs and slaves (*Saqaliba*) exchanged for Samanid silver dirhams flowing up from Khazar Atil and Central Asia.
waves.limits: Dirham hoard archaeology proves high-volume trade along the Volga–Oka–Baltic corridor; exact embarkation stages vary.

waves.title: Zhang Qian imperial diplomatic mission: Chang'an to Fergana & Bactria (138–126 BCE)
waves.summary: Han imperial exploration crossing the Hexi Corridor, Northern/Southern Tian Shan skirts, Fergana, and Bactria, returning via the southern Tarim oasis states.
waves.limits: Schematic corridor summarizing Shiji Ch. 123 outward northern capture and southern return tracks.

waves.title: Gan Ying mission across Parthia to the Persian Gulf / Charax (97 CE)
waves.summary: Eastern Han western mission dispatched by Ban Chao from the Tarim Basin across Arsacid Parthia to Charax Spasinu on the Persian Gulf.
waves.limits: Single outbound track based on Hou Hanshu stages through Parthia (*Anxi*) to *Tiaozhi*.

waves.title: Faxian & Xuanzang overland-maritime pilgrimage corridors: Chang'an to India & Sri Lanka (399–645 CE)
waves.summary: Combining Faxian's overland outward and Java-Sea return itinerary (399–414 CE) with Xuanzang's Tian Shan–Samarkand–Nalanda Grand Tour (629–645 CE).
waves.limits: Composite educational visualization uniting the two monumental Buddhist travel itineraries; each traveler had distinct local detours.

waves.title: Du Huan's westward captivity and maritime return: Talas to Iraq, Molin (Eritrea) & Guangzhou (751–762 CE)
waves.summary: Following capture at Talas (751 CE), Tang traveler Du Huan traversed Abbasid Iraq, Syria/Palestine borderlands, and the Red Sea coast of Africa (*Molin*) before boarding an Indian Ocean ship to Guangzhou in 762 CE.
waves.limits: Survived solely as quoted geographical extracts in Du You's Tongdian.

waves.title: Rabban Bar Sauma: Beijing to Rome, Paris & Bordeaux (1275–1288 CE)
waves.summary: Earliest recorded East-Asian-born envoy crossing the entire Eurasian landmass—from Kublai Khan's Khanbaliq (Beijing) through Ilkhanid Iran to Constantinople, Italy, France, and Gascony.
waves.limits: Schematic trans-Eurasian arc joining primary cities named in the Syriac chronicle.

waves.title: Quanzhou/Nanjing to Malindi: Wang Dayuan & Zheng He Indian Ocean voyages (1330–1433 CE)
waves.summary: Combined oceanic corridor sailed first by private Yuan merchant-scholar Wang Dayuan (1330s) and expanded by Ming Admiral Zheng He's seven treasure fleets (1405–1433 CE).
waves.limits: Only a detachment under Yang Min / Hong Bao / Zheng He fleet elements pushed to Mecca and East Africa on voyages 4–7.

territories.title: Volga Bulgaria at the Volga–Kama Confluence (c. 900–950 CE)
territories.limits: Simplified schematic settlement and seasonal pasture horizon of Almish ibn Shilki's Volga Bulgar confederation at the Middle Volga–Kama junction; nomads moved seasonally and no fixed linear borders existed in 922 CE.

territories.title: Khazar Khaganate Core Steppe–Delta Suzerainty (c. 900–950 CE)
territories.limits: Schematic envelope of Lower Volga–North Caucasus–Don core lands paying direct tribute to the Khazar Khaganate when Ibn Fadlan reached Volga Bulgaria in 922 CE; northern forest-steppe client zones are not drawn.

studies.title: Ahmad ibn Fadlan: the 921–922 Volga embassy
studies.summary: Follow Caliph al-Muqtadir's historical embassy from Baghdad through Samanid Bukhara, frozen Khwarazm, and Oghuz camps to Volga Bulgaria and Rus' river traders in 921–922 CE—contrasting verifiable Mashhad manuscript evidence with Crichton's Eaters of the Dead.

studies.title: Chinese Explorers: Zhang Qian to Zheng He and Xu Xiake
studies.summary: Trace 1,780 years of imperial envoys, Buddhist scholar-pilgrims, Tang captives, Mongol-era diplomats, and Ming ocean and karst surveyors across Eurasia and the Indian Ocean (138 BCE–1640 CE).
